rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās recounts that the midwife loved and warned Moses’ mother; his sister hid him in a lit furnace God cooled; later a carpenter’s failed attempts to expose the mother signaled divine intervention.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لما قربت ولادة أم موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-taqāṭ means Pharaoh’s household found and took Moses without seeking him.
rows.anchor: أي أصابوه وأخذوه من غير طلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase describes the eventual outcome, not their purpose in taking Moses: a person may earn wealth that brings ruin without intending it.
rows.anchor: لا أنهم أخذوه لهذا كما يقال لمن كسب مالا فأداه ذلك إلى الحتف والهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh, Hāmān, and their troops disobeyed God in their actions.
rows.anchor: أي عاصين ربهم في أفعالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Nile carried the chest to Pharaoh and his wife; Āsiya opened it and loved Moses. She was an Israelite of prophetic descent, compassionate and charitable to believers.
rows.anchor: وكانت آسية بنت مزاحم امرأة من بني إسرائيل استنكحها فرعون وهي من خيار النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āsiya argued that the baby was older than the year’s class of infants ordered killed and asked Pharaoh to spare him, hoping to raise him as a son; Pharaoh had no son.
rows.anchor: وإنما قالت ذلك لأنه لم يكن له ولد فأطمعته في الولد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Pharaoh learned an Israelite had killed an Egyptian and ordered a search; the next day Moses met the Israelite again as he sought Moses’ help.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لما فشا أمر قتل القبطي قيل لفرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses calls him manifestly imprudent because he fought one person yesterday and another today; this means futile opposition to Pharaoh’s numerous people, not error in religion.
rows.anchor: أي ظاهر الغواية حيث قاتلت بالأمس رجلا

words: أَن يَبْطِشَ بِٱلَّذِى هُوَ عَدُوٌّۭ لَّهُمَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses felt compassion for the Israelite and meant to seize and repel their Egyptian enemy; the Israelite mistook Moses’ rebuke as a threat to himself.
rows.anchor: فلما أخذته الرقة على الإسرائيلي وأراد أن يدفع القبطي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most exegetes say the Israelite spoke, thinking Moses meant to attack him.
rows.anchor: بالأمس عن ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan instead says the Egyptian spoke, since the killing had become widely known and he thought an Israelite had killed the man the day before.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هو من قول القبطي لأنه قد اشتهر أمر القتل بالأمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here a jabbār is one who seeks dominance through killing and oppression.
rows.anchor: أي ما تريد إلا أن تكون عاليا في الأرض بالقتل والظلم

rows.speaker: عكرمة والشعبي
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Shaʿbī say a person is called a tyrant only after killing two people unjustly.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة والشعبي: لا يكون الإنسان جبارا حتى يقتل نفسين بغير حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Egyptian recognized Moses as the killer, informed Pharaoh, and Pharaoh ordered Moses killed and sent men to find him.
rows.anchor: علم القبطي أن القاتل موسى فانطلق إلى فرعون وأخبر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man came from the city’s far edge, took a nearby shortcut to reach Moses first, and hurried to warn him.
rows.anchor: أي آخرها فاختصر طريقا قريبا حتى سبقهم إلى موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man is identified as Ḥizqīl, the believer in Pharaoh’s household; other reports name him Shimʿūn or Samʿān.
rows.anchor: وكان الرجل حزقيل مؤمن آل فرعون. وقيل: رجل اسمه شمعون

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda explains yaʾtamirūna as the nobles consulting together about Moses.
rows.anchor: أي يتشاورون فيك عن أبي عبيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that some of the nobles were ordering others.
rows.anchor: عن أبي عبيدة. وقيل: يأمر بعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is to leave Egypt; Arabic permits both naṣaḥtuhu and naṣaḥtu lahu for ‘I advised him.’
rows.anchor: في هذا يقال نصحته ونصحت له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutʿa is a benefit bringing immediate pleasure; manfaʿa may instead involve pain whose eventual consequence is beneficial. Every pleasure is a benefit, but not every benefit is pleasure.
rows.anchor: المتعة منفعة توجب الالتذاذ في الحال والمنفعة قد تكون بألم تؤدي عاقبته إلى نفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥḍār is making something present where it can be seen.
rows.anchor: والإحضار إيجاد ما به يكون الشيء بحيث يشاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaʿm is a statement based on conjecture or knowledge, so it belongs with verbs of knowing; the cited poem witnesses the usage.
rows.anchor: فإن تزعميني كنت أجهل فيكم فإني شريت الحلم بعدك بالجهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One occasion report identifies the promised person as the Messenger and the contrasting person as Abū Jahl.
rows.anchor: نزل قوله أفمن وعدناه الآية في رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبي جهل

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب والسدي
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Suddī report that the comparison is Ḥamza and ʿAlī versus Abū Jahl.
rows.anchor: عن محمد بن كعب والسدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers a general application to anyone matching the stated qualities rather than restricting the verse to particular people.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن يكون عاما فيمن يكون بهذه الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised person will certainly attain Paradise’s reward for obedience, unlike one given worldly wealth who is brought to judgment and punishment; afterlife blessings endure without grief or decay.
rows.anchor: أي فهو واصل إليه ومدركه لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s call to unbelievers on Judgment Day is a rebuke and humiliation, asking where the partners they claimed were divine and worshipped as helpers are.
rows.anchor: وهذا نداء تقريع وتبكيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those condemned include jinn and devils, as well as human beings who led others astray; they call their followers the people whom they misled.
rows.anchor: أي حق عليهم الوعيد بالعذاب من الجن والشياطين والذين أغووا الخلق من الإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders say they invited followers to error just as they themselves went astray, and they disavow the followers and their deeds.
rows.anchor: أي أضللناهم عن الدين بدعائنا إياهم إلى الضلال كما ضللنا نحن بأنفسنا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the leaders disown one another and become enemies, as in 43:67.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: برئ بعضهم من بعض وصاروا أعداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The misleaders deny that followers worshipped them: the followers worshipped devils who adorned that worship for them.
rows.anchor: أي لم يكونوا يعبدوننا بل كانوا يعبدون الشياطين الذين زينوا لهم عبادتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the followers did not worship the misleaders with any rightful claim or proof.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه لم يعبدونا باستحقاق وحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The followers are told to summon the beings they worshipped to rescue them from God’s punishment; they are called partners only because the followers falsely claimed partnership by worship.
rows.anchor: وإنما أضاف الشركاء إليهم لأنه لا يجوز أن يكون لله شريك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They call the alleged partners, who do not grant their plea, and they see the punishment.
rows.anchor: أي فيدعونهم فلا يجيبونهم إلى ملتمسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional’s answer is omitted; the author prefers ‘if they had been guided, they would have recognized the punishment as true,’ since the context signals the ellipsis.
rows.anchor: جواب لو محذوف تقديره لو أنهم كانوا يهتدون لرأوا العذاب

rows.speaker: حفص عن عاصم ويعقوب وسهل
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Yaʿqūb, and Sahl read with fatḥ on khāʾ and sīn.
rows.anchor: قرأ حفص عن عاصم ويعقوب وسهل لخسف الخاء والسين

rows.speaker: الحسن والأعرج وشيبة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿraj, Shayba, and Mujāhid also read with fatḥ on khāʾ and sīn.
rows.anchor: وهو قراءة الحسن والأعرج وشيبة ومجاهد

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The remaining readers use the passive form, with ḍamma on khāʾ and kasra on sīn.
rows.anchor: والباقون لخسف بضم الخاء وكسر السين

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the active reading follows the preceding mention of God; the passive form reaches the same meaning.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: من قرأ الخسف بنا بفتح الخاء فلتقدم ذكر الله تعالى

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb pauses after way and then starts again with anna.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يعقوب ويك يقف عليها ثم يبتدي فيقول أنه

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī records three parses: the full expression is one word, the reader pauses after way, or wayk forms a unit.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جني في ويكأنه ثلاثة أقوال منهم من جعلها كلمة واحدة

rows.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: The author favors al-Khalīl and Sībawayh: way is an exclamatory expression separate from kaʾanna, conveying amazement that unbelievers do not prosper.
rows.anchor: والوجه فيه عندنا هو قول الخليل وسيبويه وهو أن وي اسم سمي به الفعل في الخبر

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan treats wayk as a unit meaning ‘I am amazed that’; kāf is an address particle like in dhālika and ulāʾika, supported by ʿAntara’s poem.
rows.anchor: وهو قول أبي الحسن وينبغي أن يكون الكاف هنا حرف خطاب

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī notes that kaʾanna may be used without a real comparison, as in his poem describing a lovesick speaker at evening.
rows.anchor: ومما جاءت فيه كأن عارية من مضى التشبيه ما أنشده أبو علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baghy is unjustly seeking rebellion; unjust rulers are consequently called bughāt.
rows.anchor: البغي طلب العتو بغير حق ومنه قيل لولاة الجور بغاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kanz is accumulated wealth, conventionally hidden underground; legally only wealth on which zakāt is unpaid is called a treasure, given the warning about it.
rows.anchor: والكنز جمع المال بعضه على بعض وصار بالعرف عبارة عما يخبأ تحت الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mafātiḥ and mafātīḥ are plural forms with the same meaning: what opens a lock.
rows.anchor: والمفاتح جمع مفتح والمفاتيح جمع مفتاح ومعناهما واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāʾa bi-ḥimlihi means to rise under its weight; anʾāʾ is also used. An ʿuṣba is a tightly joined group.
rows.anchor: وناء بحمله ينوء نوءا إذا نهض به مع ثقله عليه

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd says nāʾanī al-ḥiml means ‘the load weighed me down.’
rows.anchor: وقال أبو زيد: ناءني الحمل إذا أثقلني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāʾ and hamza can alternate in transitive forms; Arabic says the keys weigh down a group or, in the inverse form, the group bears them.
rows.anchor: فالباء والهمز يتعاقبان في تعدي الفعل قال سبحانه

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda interprets the phrase as inverted order, meaning the group is weighed down by the keys; the author rejects this as incorrect and unsuitable for Qurʾānic language.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: هذا من المقلوب ومعنى قوله لتنوء بالعصبة تنوء العصبة بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects using alleged poetic inversions to explain Qurʾānic wording, since examples may be Arab poetic errors; he cites the lamp and Imruʾ al-Qays lines as such cases.
rows.anchor: وهذا غير صحيح ولا يجوز أن يحمل القرآن عليه لأنه يجري مجرى الغلط من العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anonymous lamp poem is offered as an inversion example: ‘the eye shines by it’ is taken to mean ‘it makes the eye shine.’
rows.anchor: إن سراجا لكريم مفخره تجلى به العين إذا ما تجهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s line about an oil lamp in lamp-wicks is another alleged inversion example.
rows.anchor: يضيء الظلام وجهها لضجيعها كمصباح زيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited line about a thrust by Ḥuṣayn is treated as an example in which an object is expressed as the agent.
rows.anchor: غداة أحلت لابن صرمة طعنة حصين غبيطات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rājiz’s verse mistakenly treats pistachios as vegetables, further showing that poetry can contain errors.
rows.anchor: جارية لم تعلم المرققا ولم تذق من البقول الفستقا

rows.speaker: خداش بن زهير
rows.claim: Although many read Khidāsh’s line as saying men suffer from spears, the author says the spears suffer because they are too noble to be used against such thugs.
rows.anchor: وتركت خيلا لا هوادة بينها وتشقى الرماح بالضياطرة الحمر

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s ‘red one of ʿĀd’ is no mistake for Thamūd: Thamūd was called the later ʿĀd, descended from survivors of the first ʿĀd; their name evokes scant water and smaller numbers.
rows.anchor: فتنتج لكم غلمان أشأم كلهم كأحمر عاد ثم تنتج فتتئم

words: إِنَّ قَٰرُونَ كَانَ مِن قَوْمِ مُوسَىٰ
rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says Qarun was an Israelite from Moses’ tribe and his maternal cousin; a report from Abū ʿAbd Allāh agrees.
rows.anchor: أي كان من بني إسرائيل ثم من سبط موسى وهو ابن خالته عن عطاء عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj instead makes Qarun Moses’ paternal cousin based on their descent from Qāhath.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان ابن عم موسى لحا لأنه كان قارون بن يصهر بن قاهث وموسى بن عمران بن قاهث عن ابن جريج

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq says Moses was Qarun’s nephew and Qarun his uncle.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كل موسى ابن أخيه وقارون عمه عن محمد بن إسحاق

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says Qarun lorded his treasures over the Israelites; he was called al-Munawwar for his beauty and, despite being a foremost Torah reciter, hypocritically rebelled like al-Sāmirī.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة قال وكان يسمي المنور لحسن صورته

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب وابن عباس
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn ʿAbbās say Qarun was Pharaoh’s agent over the Israelites in Egypt and oppressed them.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن المسيب وابن عباس

rows.speaker: عطاء الخراساني وشهر بن حوشب
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab say Qarun added a span to his clothes.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه زاد عليهم في الثياب شبرا عن عطاء الخراساني وشهر بن حوشب

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says Qarun found one of Joseph’s hidden treasures.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء أصاب كنزا من كنوز يوسف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Most exegetes, including Ibn ʿAbbās, take the keys as Qarun’s treasuries; al-Zajjāj prefers this view, comparing the phrase with 6:59.
rows.anchor: فيكون المراد بمفاتحه خزائن ماله وهو قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Qatāda and Mujāhid instead understand the keys as implements for opening doors.
rows.anchor: هي المفاتح التي تفتح بها الأبواب عن قتادة ومجاهد

rows.speaker: الأعمش عن خيثمة
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash transmits from Khaythama that Qarun’s leather keys were each as large as a finger.
rows.anchor: وروى الأعمش عن خيثمة قال: كانت مفاتيح قارون من جلود كل مفتاح مثل الإصبع

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid defines an ʿuṣba as ten to fifteen people.
rows.anchor: ما بين عشرة إلى خمسة عشرة عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda defines an ʿuṣba as ten to forty people.
rows.anchor: ما بين عشرة إلى أربعين عن قتادة

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ says an ʿuṣba is forty men.
rows.anchor: أربعون رجلا عن أبي صالح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines an ʿuṣba as three to ten people.
rows.anchor: ما بين الثلاثة إلى العشرة عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is any group whose members support one another.
rows.anchor: إنهم الجماعة يتعصب بعضهم لبعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarun’s people tell him not to exult boastfully, swagger, or act arrogantly over his treasures; God does not love that disposition.
rows.anchor: أي لا تأشر ولا تمرح ولا تتكبر بسبب كنوزك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anonymous poems show farḥ can mean insolent boasting rather than ordinary happiness.
rows.anchor: ولست بمفراح إذا الدهر سرني ولا جازع من صرفه المتقلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The advice is usually attributed to Qarun’s believing kinsmen; another view says Moses addressed him in the plural.
rows.anchor: وهذا أيضا من مقالة المؤمنين من قوم قارون له. وقيل: إن المخاطب له بذلك موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Use God’s wealth to seek the afterlife by spending it on good works and charity.
rows.anchor: اطلب فيما أعطاك الله من الأموال الدار الآخرة بأن تنفقها في سبيل الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes take this to mean doing worldly deeds for the afterlife: one’s true share of this life is what benefits the next.
rows.anchor: وهو أن تعمل في الدنيا للآخرة عن أكثر المفسرين ومعناه لا تنس أن تعمل لآخرتك

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī explains one’s worldly share as health, strength, free time, youth, energy, and wealth, which one should use to seek the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وروي في معناه عن علي ع لا تنس صحتك وقوتك وفراغك وشبابك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Qarun was told to give away the surplus while retaining enough to suffice him.
rows.anchor: أمر أن يقدم الفضل وأن يمسك ما يغنيه عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says the miserly Qarun was told he could eat, drink, and lawfully enjoy what God gave him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه أنه كان فتورا شحيحا فقيل له كل واشرب واستمتع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Give generously to people as God has been generous to Qarun.
rows.anchor: أي أفضل على الناس كما أفضل الله عليك

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Sallām says it means to fulfill God’s obligations as God has bestowed blessings.
rows.anchor: أحسن فيما افترض الله عليك كما أحسن في إنعامه عليك عن يحيى بن سلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation combines thanking God according to His blessings with supporting God’s servants through one’s wealth.
rows.anchor: معناه وأحسن شكر الله تعالى على قدر إنعامه عليك وواس عباد الله بمالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not seek to commit disobedience on earth.
rows.anchor: إن الله لا يحب المفسدين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says Qarun claimed superior knowledge and merit, supposing the wealth was God’s reward for his distinction, like the boast in 18:36.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة يعني أنه قدر أن هذا ثواب من الله له لفضيلته

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Qarun meant God favored him because He knew he deserved the wealth; this is close to Qatāda’s view.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه لرضا الله عني ومعرفته باستحقاقي عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view is that Qarun meant specialized knowledge of trade, agriculture, and other ways of making wealth unavailable to others.
rows.anchor: المال حصل له على علم عندي بوجوه المكاسب وبما لا يتهيأ لأحد

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says Qarun claimed knowledge of gold-making or alchemy; a story says Moses, Joshua, and Aaron’s son each taught him a third, and Qarun tricked them into revealing all three.
rows.anchor: وهو علم الكيمياء عن الكلبي وحكي أن موسى ع علم قارون الثلث

words: أَوَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ قَدْ أَهْلَكَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God destroyed unbelieving generations stronger and wealthier than Qarun, including ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Lot’s people; wealth could not save them from punishment.
rows.anchor: أهلك من قبله من القرون

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says criminals enter Hell without being called to account.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: يعني أنهم يدخلون النار بغير حساب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda also says angels recognize criminals by their marks, seize them by forelocks and feet, and drive them to Hell, as in 55:39.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: إن الملائكة تعرفهم بسيماهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reconciles this with 15:92: that questioning is rebuke and reproach, not a request for information.
rows.anchor: لا ليعلم ذلك من قبلهم عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarun went out among the Israelites in his finery with his attendants and followers.
rows.anchor: أي خرج قارون على بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda describes four thousand riding beasts with four thousand riders, all in purple; arjawān is a red dye.
rows.anchor: في أربعة آلاف دابة عليها أربعة آلاف فارس عليهم وعلى دوابهم الأرجوان عن قتادة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī describes white maidservants on gold saddles and purple carpets, riding white mules in red garments and gold jewelry.
rows.anchor: على بغال بيض عليهن ثياب حمر وحلي من ذهب عن السدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Qarun went out with seventy thousand people wearing safflower-dyed garments.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خرج في سبعين ألفا عليهم المعصفرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who wish for worldly life include unbelievers, hypocrites, and weak believers, dazzled by Qarun’s finery and splendor.
rows.anchor: من الكفار والمنافقين وضعيفي الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They envy Qarun’s rank and wealth and call him richly fortunate in worldly life.
rows.anchor: أي ذو نصيب وافر من الدنيا والمعنى إنهم تمنوا مثل منزلته ومثل ماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those given knowledge are believers who affirm God’s promise.
rows.anchor: وهم المصدقون بوعد الله المؤمنون لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s reward is better than Qarun’s wealth; the phrase ‘what Qarun was given’ is understood from context.
rows.anchor: مما أوتي قارون وحذف لدلالة الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes ‘it’ this wise saying, which only the patient in obedience to God can receive and follow.
rows.anchor: أي ولا يلقى مثل هذه الكلمة ولا يوفق لها إلا الصابرون

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī instead takes ‘it’ to be Paradise, given to those patient in obedience and resistant to worldly glitter.
rows.anchor: إلا الصابرون على طاعة الله وعن زينة الدنيا عن الكلبي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says Qarun paid an Israelite prostitute two thousand to falsely accuse Moses of soliciting her before the Israelites; she regretted it and exposed Qarun’s slander plot and marked money.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: دعا قارون امرأة من بني إسرائيل بغيا فقال لها إني أعطيك ألفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the woman exposed Qarun’s slander, Moses invoked God, who made the earth obey him. It swallowed Qarun and his bed by stages despite his pleas for kinship; God says Qarun would have been saved had he called on Him.
rows.anchor: فعرف بنو إسرائيل خاتم قارون فغضب موسى فدعا الله عليه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says the Israelites accused Moses of swallowing Qarun to inherit his wealth because they were cousins; his house and all property were swallowed three days later and never recovered.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: ولما أمر موسى الأرض فابتلعته

words: فَمَا كَانَ لَهُۥ مِن فِئَةٍۢ يَنصُرُونَهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No group devoted to Qarun could ward off God’s punishment; he had trusted his retinue and troops but could not save himself either.
rows.anchor: لأنه كان يقدر مع نفسه الامتناع بحاشيته وجنوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who had envied Qarun the day before now speak with regret and admit that God expands or restricts provision as He wills.
rows.anchor: وهذه كلمة ندم واعتراف وقد بينا

rows.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh separate way from kaʾanna; the expression can be said by someone recognizing an error.
rows.anchor: عند الخليل وسيبويه لفظة وي مفصولة من كأن

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ derives wayk from waylak with the lām deleted, and takes anna as accusative after an omitted verb meaning ‘I know that God…’
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: أصله ويلك فحذفت اللام وجعلت أن مفتوحة

rows.speaker: شيخ من أهل البصرة
rows.claim: A Basran informant quotes a Bedouin woman saying wayk innahu, meaning ‘do you not see? He is behind the house.’
rows.anchor: وحدثني شيخ من أهل البصرة قال سمعت أعرابية تقول لزوجها

rows.speaker: الكسائي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī, attributing the reading to Ibn ʿAbbās, glosses it ‘that is, God’: provision rises or falls by wisdom, not as a measure of honor or disgrace.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: ويكأن في التأويل ذلك إن الله وهو قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda gloss waykaʾanna as ‘do you not know?’
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وقتادة: ويكأن معناه ألم تعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says that if God had not favored them by withholding Qarun’s wealth, they too would have been swallowed; another says mercy forgave their wish for Qarun’s rank.
rows.anchor: أي لولا أنه أنعم علينا بنعمه فلم يعطنا ما أعطى قارون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deny God’s blessings and worship others alongside Him do not attain reward or escape punishment.
rows.anchor: أي لا يفوز بثواب الله وينجو من عقابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarun’s story continues the promised account of Moses: it is another episode from Moses’ story.
rows.anchor: إنما اتصلت قصة قارون بما قبلها من قوله نتلو عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Qarun’s story reinforces that worldly goods are temporary and what is with God is better and more enduring, as stated in 42:36.
rows.anchor: فأكد سبحانه ذلك بحديث قارون وحاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another connection is that, after describing unbelievers’ disgrace on Judgment Day, the commentary identifies Qarun as one of them, to be disgraced then as he was in this life.
rows.anchor: ذكر عقيبة أن قارون من جملتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indecency is men having sex with men.
rows.anchor: ثم فسر الفاحشة بقوله { إنكم لتأتون الرجال } أي تنكحونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that preferring men to women cuts off procreation.
rows.anchor: أحدها: تقطعون سبيل الولد باختياركم الرجال على النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second account says they attacked passing travelers: they stoned them by lot, seized the person hit, took his property, sodomized him, charged three dirhams, and had a judge rule on it.
rows.anchor: وثانيها: إنكم تقطعون الناس عن الأسفار بإتيان هذه الفاحشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation is that they robbed people on the road like highway bandits.
rows.anchor: وثالثها: إنهم كانوا يقطعون الطريق على الناس كما يفعل قطاع الطريق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وروي عن الرضا
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, with a report also from al-Riḍā, says they farted in their gatherings without modesty or shame.
rows.anchor: أحدها: هو أنهم كانوا يتضارطون في مجالسهم من غير حشمة ولا حياء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they had sex with men in their assemblies in full view of one another.
rows.anchor: وثانيها: أنهم كانوا يأتون الرجال في مجالسهم يرى بعضهم بعضا عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view lists public indecencies: insults, buffoonery, slapping, gambling, stick-fighting, stone-throwing, music, exposure, and sodomy.
rows.anchor: كانت مجالسهم تشتمل على أنواع من المناكير والقبائح مثل الشتم والسخف والصفع

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj draws a lesson: people should not socialize around indecencies or gather to commit forbidden acts.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وفي هذا إعلام أنه لا ينبغي أن يتعاشر الناس على المناكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Lot condemned their disgraceful acts, they mocked him by demanding God’s punishment; Lot then prayed for help against the corrupt people who committed sins and spread corruption.
rows.anchor: ولما أنكر لوط على قومه ما كانوا يأتونه من الفضائح قالوا له استهزاء ائتنا بعذاب الله
